title: Distributed systems: how things fail
tagline: Partial failure, and the small set of patterns that keep one slow service from taking everything down.
why: Most large outages start small: one slow query, one dependency that hangs, one recovery that gets flattened by retries. The patterns in this day decide whether that small fault stays small. When you are debugging an outage, knowing how failure spreads tells you to look for the first thing that got slow, not the loudest thing that is broken.
objectives: Say what a timeout tells you about a remote call, and what it does not
Check a call chain's timeouts and retries against the user-facing deadline and find the hop that breaks the budget
Calculate how retries at several layers multiply load, and explain how jitter prevents a second outage after recovery
Trace a cascading failure back to the first slow dependency, and name the pattern that would have contained it
Choose between two-phase commit and a saga for an action that spans services

blocks.text: Inside one process, a function call either returns or raises. Across a network, a call can succeed, fail, or time out, and a timeout does not tell you which of the first two happened. This is **partial failure**: some parts of the system work while others do not, and a caller often cannot tell which.

Engineers at Sun Microsystems wrote down a list of assumptions that people make about networks and that are false. They are worth reading as a checklist, because almost every distributed-systems bug traces back to one of them.

blocks.caption: Relay calls the payment provider to issue a refund
rows: It was refused, if the error is from the provider
Ask the provider, or retry with the same key
blocks.verdict: Treat a timeout as unknown. Design calls with side effects so that asking again, or retrying with the same idempotency key, settles the outcome.

blocks.title: Two sides of the same refund
blocks.code:
relay-api   10:14:02.000 POST https://payments.example/refunds key=rf_9921 start
relay-api   10:14:12.001 refund rf_9921 TIMEOUT after 10.0s, marking failed
relay-api   10:14:12.004 retrying refund for ticket 9921 with key=rf_9921b

payments    10:14:02.140 refund key=rf_9921 received
payments    10:14:12.150 refund key=rf_9921b received
payments    10:14:13.870 refund key=rf_9921 completed amount=39.00
payments    10:14:14.020 refund key=rf_9921b completed amount=39.00
notes: Relay gave up at 10 seconds. The provider finished the first refund at about 11.9 seconds. Both statements are true.
Relay logged 'failed', which was wrong. A timeout should be recorded as unknown.
The retry used a new key, so the provider treated it as a different refund. Reusing `rf_9921` would have returned the first result instead.

blocks.text: Slow is worse than down. A service that is down refuses connections within milliseconds, and the caller moves on. A service that is slow holds every caller's thread, connection, and memory while they wait. Callers pile up behind it, and their own callers pile up behind them.

blocks.title: Logging a timeout as a failure
blocks.text: A timeout means the caller stopped waiting. The remote side may still finish the work. Code that marks a timed-out refund as failed and then retries with a fresh key produces exactly the double refund in the log above.

blocks.title: The LLM API is the slowest dependency Relay has
blocks.text: A database query takes milliseconds; an LLM call can take tens of seconds, and its latency varies with output length and provider load. When the provider slows down, every Relay worker holding an open LLM call is stuck, which is the 'slow is worse than down' case in its purest form.

blocks.q: Relay's call to the payment provider times out after 10 seconds. What does Relay know about the refund?
options: It failed, because no success response arrived
It may or may not have happened
It succeeded, because the request was sent
blocks.explain: The request may have been lost, processed and the reply lost, or still be running. The timeout only says Relay stopped waiting, so the outcome must be checked or the call retried with the same idempotency key.

blocks.prompt: Why does a dependency that refuses connections usually cause less damage upstream than one that accepts connections and then hangs?
blocks.answer: A refused connection fails in milliseconds, so the caller's thread is free at once and it can return an error or a fallback. A hang holds the caller's thread and connection until a timeout fires, and if there is no timeout, forever. Held resources are what spread the failure.

blocks.text: Every remote call needs a **timeout**, a limit on how long the caller will wait. Some clients have no limit by default: Python's `requests` library waits indefinitely unless you pass a timeout. A call with no timeout turns any hang downstream into a hang in your service.

options.name: Long timeout
cost: Threads and connections held during a hang
Callers upstream may give up first anyway
options.choose: Choose this for work with no user waiting, such as a batch job, and for calls known to be slow, such as a long LLM generation.

options.name: Short timeout
gain: Frees resources fast when a dependency hangs
cost: Cuts off the slow tail of healthy calls
options.choose: Choose this on the path of a user request, set a little above the dependency's normal p99.

blocks.text: A timeout budget across a call chain

A request passes through several hops, each with its own timeout. The **timeout budget** is the user-facing deadline divided among them. Each hop must finish within the time its caller has left. When an inner timeout is longer than an outer one, the outer layer gives up and returns an error while the inner layer keeps working on a request nobody will receive.

blocks.title: Relay's chat request: worked budget
blocks.code:
BEFORE                timeout  attempts  worst case
load balancer             30s        1        30s
nginx -> API              60s        1        60s
API -> pgvector search     5s        3        15s
API -> LLM API            60s        3       180s
worst case inside API: 15s + 180s = 195s; the user got a 504 at 30s

AFTER                 timeout  attempts  worst case
load balancer             30s        1        30s
nginx -> API              29s        1        29s
API deadline              28s, set when the request arrives
API -> pgvector search   1.5s        2         3s
API -> LLM API      20s or time left     1        20s
worst case inside API: 3s + 20s = 23s, under the 28s deadline
notes: Worst case for one hop is timeout times attempts, before any backoff waits. Before the fix, the LLM hop alone was six times the user's deadline.
After the fix, every layer is shorter than the layer above it, with a margin for processing.
The API passes the time left to each call instead of a fixed number, so a slow search leaves less for the LLM, not more total time.
LLM retries moved out of the request. A failed generation now returns a clear error, or goes to a queue.

blocks.text: Retry only failures that are likely to be transient, such as a timeout, a 503, or a 429, and only operations that are safe to repeat: reads, or writes carrying an idempotency key. Wait longer before each attempt with **exponential backoff**, for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds, capped. Add **jitter**, a random amount, so that clients that failed together do not retry together.
Retry storms

blocks.title: Retry amplification, worked
blocks.code:
Retries at every layer, 3 attempts each, database down:
  web app -> API -> tools service -> Postgres
  attempts reaching Postgres per user action = 3 x 3 x 3 = 27
  normal 200 actions/s  ->  up to 5,400 queries/s at the database

Synchronized retries after an outage, no jitter:
  10,000 clients waiting, each retries on a fixed timer
  service returns at capacity 2,000 req/s
  first second: 10,000 retries + new traffic -> overloaded again

Same clients with retries spread at random over 30s:
  10,000 / 30 = about 333 extra req/s on top of normal traffic
notes: Retries multiply across layers. Retry at one layer, usually the outermost one that knows whether the user still cares.
A **retry storm** is retry traffic large enough to keep a recovering service down. Without jitter, the retries arrive as one wave.
A retry budget, such as allowing retries up to 10 percent of normal traffic, caps the extra load no matter how many calls fail.

blocks.title: Recovery followed by a second outage
blocks.text: Plot request rate across the recovery moment. A rate several times normal, in spikes at a fixed interval, with most requests marked as retries, is a retry storm. Confirm with retry-attempt counts in access logs or client metrics. The fix is backoff with jitter on the clients and load shedding at the edge until the wave passes.

blocks.title: Timeouts for a slow, costly dependency
blocks.text: With streaming, set two limits: time to first token, and the longest allowed gap between chunks, instead of one total timeout that a long valid answer can exceed. Every retry of a generation costs tokens and adds the full latency again. When the provider returns an overload error, fast retries from every client add to the overload.

blocks.q: The web app, the API, and the tools service each make up to 3 attempts. Postgres is down. How many queries can one user action send to Postgres?
blocks.explain: Each of the web app's 3 attempts causes 3 API attempts, and each of those causes 3 tools-service attempts: 3 times 3 times 3. Adding attempts at each layer multiplies them.

blocks.prompt: Ten thousand clients all retry on a fixed 5-second timer. Why does adding jitter help even though the total number of retries is unchanged?
blocks.answer: The service fails on peak rate, not on totals. Without jitter, the retries arrive in the same second as one wave far above capacity. Spread randomly over a window, the same retries become a modest extra rate the service can absorb.

lessons.title: Circuit breakers, bulkheads, and load shedding

blocks.text: Timeouts and retries protect a single call. Four more patterns protect a whole service from a dependency in trouble: stop calling it for a while, keep its trouble in its own compartment, refuse work you cannot finish, and keep offering a reduced service. Without them, one slow component becomes a **cascading failure**, where each layer's distress causes the next layer's.

blocks.title: A cascading failure in Relay, step by step

steps.label: One query becomes slow
steps.detail: A deploy changes the `lookup_order` query so it no longer uses an index. It now takes about 8 seconds instead of 20 milliseconds.
steps.fail: p99 latency of `lookup_order` jumps. Nothing else looks wrong yet.

steps.label: The connection pool fills
steps.detail: Each order lookup holds a database connection for 8 seconds. The pool, shared by every endpoint, runs out.
steps.fail: Logs show pool timeouts: requests waiting for a connection give up.

steps.label: Every worker is waiting
steps.detail: All API workers or threads are blocked on the pool. Endpoints that never touch orders queue behind them.
steps.fail: Help-center search and login slow down although they use healthy tables.

steps.label: Health checks time out
steps.detail: The health endpoint waits in the same queue and misses its deadline. Instances are marked unhealthy and removed.
steps.fail: 502 and 504 rates climb; instances flap in and out of rotation.

steps.label: Clients retry
steps.detail: The web app retries each 504 up to three times, and the remaining instances take the extra load.
steps.fail: Request rate rises while the success rate falls.

steps.label: Jobs time out and requeue
steps.detail: Triage jobs that call the API time out and are retried, adding more load.
steps.fail: Queue depth climbs, and the backlog will hit the API on recovery.

steps.label: Total outage
steps.detail: Every user-facing feature fails. The root cause is one query on one table.
steps.fail: The incident looks like 'everything broke at once', which hides where it started.

blocks.caption: Patterns that contain a failing dependency
columns: Where it cuts the cascade above
rows: Stops calling a failing dependency for a cooldown, failing at once
Order lookups fail fast instead of holding connections
Some calls fail that might have succeeded
Gives each dependency its own pool of connections or workers
Order lookups exhaust only their own pool
Pools sized separately; idle capacity in each
Accepted requests still finish within the deadline
Serves a reduced feature when a part fails
Chat answers without order status instead of failing
More code paths to build and test
blocks.verdict: Use timeouts everywhere, bulkheads around dependencies that can hang, circuit breakers on calls that fail in bursts, and load shedding at the edge.

blocks.text: A **circuit breaker** has three states. Closed: calls pass through and failures are counted. Open: after failures cross a threshold, calls fail immediately for a cooldown period, without touching the dependency. Half-open: after the cooldown, a few trial calls go through; success closes the breaker, failure opens it again.

options.name: Retry
cost: Multiplies load on a struggling dependency
Adds latency to every failed call
options.choose: Choose this when failures are rare and independent, and the operation is idempotent.

options.name: Fail fast
gain: Gives the dependency room to recover
cost: Users see errors or a degraded answer
options.choose: Choose this when failures are widespread, such as when the breaker is open or the dependency signals overload.

blocks.text: **Load shedding** means refusing work you cannot finish in time, as early and cheaply as possible, so that the work you accept succeeds. Shed the least important traffic first. For Relay, the nightly eval harness and the re-indexing jobs should be refused before a customer's chat message.

blocks.title: One slow dependency exhausts every thread upstream
blocks.text: When every endpoint slows at once, look at what the busy workers are waiting on, not at which endpoint is loudest. A stack dump of a live worker, for example with `py-spy dump`, or the in-flight spans in your tracing tool, will show nearly all of them blocked in the same call. That call's dependency is where the cascade started.

blocks.title: Health checks that test dependencies
blocks.text: If the health endpoint queries Postgres, a slow database marks every API instance unhealthy at once, and the load balancer removes them all. A failing dependency becomes a full outage. Keep the check that decides whether to restart an instance about the process itself.

blocks.q: A circuit breaker around Relay's calls to the payment provider has been open for its 30-second cooldown. What happens next?
options: It closes and lets all traffic through
It lets a few trial calls through to test the provider
It stays open until an operator resets it
blocks.explain: After the cooldown the breaker goes half-open and admits a few trial calls. Closing at once would send the full load to a provider that may still be failing, which is the mistake the half-open state exists to avoid.

blocks.prompt: In the cascade above, which single change would most likely have kept help-center search and login working?
blocks.answer: A bulkhead: a separate connection pool, or separate workers, for order lookups. The slow query would have exhausted only that pool, and every other endpoint would have kept its connections. A statement timeout on the database would also have limited how long each slow query held a connection.

blocks.text: Inside one database, a transaction makes several writes succeed or fail together. A business action that spans services, each with its own data, has no such transaction. A Relay refund touches Relay's Postgres, the payment provider, and the email provider. Any of them can fail after the others have succeeded.

**Two-phase commit** (2PC) is the classic attempt at one transaction across systems. A coordinator asks every participant to prepare, meaning to promise it can commit, while holding its locks. If all agree, the coordinator tells them all to commit. If the coordinator dies after the prepare, participants wait with locks held until it returns.

A **saga** splits the action into a sequence of local transactions, each in one service, and pairs each with a **compensating action** that undoes its effect, such as refunding a charge or cancelling an order. If a later step fails, the saga runs the compensations for the steps already done. In between, other readers can see the partial state.

options.name: Two-phase commit
cost: Every participant must support the protocol
options.choose: Choose this only inside infrastructure you control where every participant supports it, such as some databases and message brokers.

options.name: Saga
cost: Compensations must be designed and can fail too
options.choose: Choose this for business flows across services or third parties, such as order, charge, and ship.

blocks.title: Order charged but never created
blocks.code:
11:20:04.118 checkout charge ok provider_charge=ch_7781 amount=129.00
11:20:04.120 checkout inserting order for cart c_552
11:20:04.402 checkout ERROR deadlock detected, transaction rolled back
11:20:04.403 checkout returning 500 to client

reconcile 02:00 provider charges without a matching order: 3
  ch_7781  129.00  cart c_552
notes: The charge, an external effect, happened before the local write. When the write rolled back, nothing undid the charge.
A saga would record the order as pending first, charge with the order ID as idempotency key, then confirm, and refund if confirmation fails.
The nightly reconciliation job, comparing provider charges with orders, is the safety net that found it.

blocks.caption: During a network partition, each side must choose
rows: The app works, maybe with stale data
Carts, drafts, chat history, view counts
blocks.verdict: Decide per piece of data. Relay should refuse refunds it cannot record consistently, and can keep accepting chat messages.

blocks.text: Clocks on different machines disagree. Each drifts, and time-sync services such as NTP keep them close, often within milliseconds, but a clock can be further off or jump. Never order events from two machines by their wall-clock timestamps. Use one source of order, such as a database sequence or a version number, and measure durations with a monotonic clock, which never runs backwards.

Some systems need several machines to agree on one fact, such as which node is the leader. They use a consensus algorithm such as Raft or Paxos, which needs a majority, or **quorum**, to decide. Three nodes tolerate one failure; five tolerate two. Use a system that does this, such as etcd, rather than writing it yourself.

blocks.title: Timestamps from two machines disagree
blocks.text: If a worker log says a job finished before the API log says it was enqueued, suspect clock skew before suspecting causality bugs. Check the time-sync status on both hosts. Then reorder the events by something both sides share, such as a message ID with a sequence number, or a trace with parent and child spans.

blocks.title: Compensation is not undo
blocks.text: A refund is a second transaction that the customer sees on their statement. An email cannot be unsent. Order the steps of a saga so that the ones hardest to compensate come last.

blocks.q: Relay's refund flow updates Relay's database and calls an external payment provider. Why is two-phase commit not an option?
options: The provider's API does not take part in a prepare and commit protocol
Two-phase commit only works inside a single database
Two-phase commit cannot handle money amounts
blocks.explain: 2PC needs every participant to accept a prepare and hold the outcome until told to commit. A third-party HTTP API does not do that, so the flow must be a saga with idempotency keys and compensation.

blocks.prompt: A five-node consensus cluster loses two nodes. Can it still elect a leader? What about after losing three?
blocks.answer: With two lost, three of five remain, which is a majority, so it can still decide. With three lost, two remain, which is not a majority, so it stops accepting decisions rather than risk two leaders.

fieldGuide.symptom: Every endpoint is slow at once, including ones that do not use the failing feature
causes: One slow dependency holds every worker or connection in a shared pool
No timeout on a call that is hanging
fieldGuide.look: What busy workers are blocked on: a stack dump of a live worker, or in-flight spans grouped by dependency.
fieldGuide.confirm: Nearly all workers or connections are waiting in the same call, and that call's latency rose first.
fieldGuide.fix: Timeouts on that call, a bulkhead pool for it, and a statement timeout in the database. Shorter limits cut off some slow valid calls.

fieldGuide.symptom: Service recovers, then falls over again within a minute
causes: Retry storm: clients retry in sync without jitter
Queued work and backlog flushed at once on recovery
fieldGuide.look: Request rate across the recovery moment, and the share of requests that are retries.
fieldGuide.confirm: Rate several times normal, arriving in spikes at a fixed interval.
fieldGuide.fix: Exponential backoff with jitter and capped attempts on clients; shed load at the edge until the wave passes.

causes: External charge made before the local write, which then rolled back
Process died between the two steps
fieldGuide.look: The provider's charge list against orders for the same window, matched by idempotency key or cart ID.
fieldGuide.confirm: A charge exists with no matching order row.
fieldGuide.fix: Saga ordering: create the order as pending first, charge with its ID as the idempotency key, compensate on failure, and reconcile nightly.

fieldGuide.symptom: Timestamps from two machines disagree: a job finished before it was enqueued
causes: A clock jumped after a time-sync correction
fieldGuide.look: Time-sync status on both hosts, and a shared ordering source such as message IDs or trace spans.
fieldGuide.confirm: The offset between hosts roughly equals the impossible gap in the logs.
fieldGuide.fix: Fix time sync, order by a sequence or version, and measure durations with a monotonic clock.

fieldGuide.symptom: Client timed out, but the action happened anyway, sometimes twice
causes: The callee finished after the caller gave up
Retry sent with a new idempotency key
fieldGuide.look: Callee logs for the request after the caller's timeout moment.
fieldGuide.confirm: The callee completed the first request after the caller's timeout, and again on the retry.
fieldGuide.fix: Treat timeouts as unknown, reuse the same idempotency key on retry, and check status before acting again.

fieldGuide.symptom: 504 from the load balancer while the API logs the same request finishing with 200 later
causes: Inner timeouts longer than the outer deadline
Retries inside the request exceed the budget
fieldGuide.look: The timeout and attempt count at each hop compared with the load balancer's limit.
fieldGuide.confirm: API completion time for the request is beyond the load balancer's timeout.
fieldGuide.fix: Set a deadline at entry, pass the remaining time to each call, and keep each hop shorter than its caller.

fieldGuide.symptom: LLM calls hang for minutes with no error
causes: Streaming call with no limit on the gap between chunks
fieldGuide.look: The client's timeout configuration, and in-flight call durations.
fieldGuide.confirm: Calls stuck far beyond the provider's normal latency, with no timeout ever firing.
fieldGuide.fix: Set connect, first-token, and idle-gap timeouts. Too short and long valid answers get cut off.

fieldGuide.symptom: Load balancer removes all instances at once while one dependency is slow
causes: Health check queries a dependency, so its slowness fails every instance's check
fieldGuide.look: What the health endpoint calls, and its latency during the incident.
fieldGuide.confirm: Health checks fail on every instance at the same time the dependency slowed.
fieldGuide.fix: Keep restart decisions about the process itself; report dependency trouble through metrics and degraded responses.

fieldGuide.symptom: Two scheduler instances both run the nightly job
causes: Both believe they are leader after a network split or a lock that expired
fieldGuide.look: Scheduler logs on each instance for leadership claims and lock renewals.
fieldGuide.confirm: Both instances log that they hold leadership for overlapping periods.
fieldGuide.fix: Use a lease from a consensus-backed store, check a fencing token before acting, and make the job idempotent.

glossary.def: Some components of a system fail while others keep working, and callers often cannot tell which parts succeeded.
A limit on how long a caller waits for a response. When it fires, the outcome of the call is unknown, not failed.
The user-facing deadline divided across the hops of a call chain, so each hop finishes within the time its caller has left.
A random amount added to a retry wait so that clients that failed together do not retry together.
Retry traffic large enough to overload a dependency, often keeping it down after it recovers, or multiplied across layers.
A cap on retries as a fraction of normal traffic, so failures cannot multiply load without limit.
A failure that spreads from one component to the layers that depend on it, usually through exhausted threads, connections, or retries.
A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a cooldown, then admits a few trial calls before resuming.
A separate pool of connections or workers per dependency, so one dependency's trouble cannot exhaust shared resources.
Rejecting excess or low-priority work early, usually with 503, so the work that is accepted completes in time.
A protocol where a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then to commit, giving one outcome. Blocks if the coordinator fails mid-way.
A multi-service action built from local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes its effect if a later step fails.
The difference between the clocks of two machines. Makes cross-machine wall-clock timestamps unreliable for ordering events.
A majority of nodes in a cluster. Consensus systems need a quorum to decide, so a cluster of 2n+1 nodes tolerates n failures.

apply.title: Draw the timeout budget of one of your own requests
steps: Pick one request path in your project that calls an LLM API, and list every remote call it makes, in order.
For each call, find the timeout and the number of retries actually configured, including library defaults. Mark any call with no timeout.
Multiply timeout by attempts for each hop and add them up. Compare the total with how long a user or calling script would really wait.
Find every place that retries. If more than one layer retries the same call, write down the worst-case number of attempts that reach the provider.

quiz.q: A service calls a payment API to create a charge and gets no response before its 10-second timeout. What can it conclude about the charge?
options: It failed, since no success was returned
It succeeded, since the request was sent
Its outcome is unknown and must be checked
It was rejected, since the API is overloaded
quiz.explain: A timeout only means the caller stopped waiting. The request may have been lost, completed with the reply lost, or still be running. Treating it as a failure and retrying without the same idempotency key is how double charges happen.
why: The charge may have completed after the caller stopped waiting.
The request may never have arrived, or may have been refused.
Nothing in a timeout says why; overload is one possibility among several.

quiz.context: Users see intermittent 504 errors from Relay's chat. The load balancer's timeout is 30 seconds.

artifact.title: load balancer and API logs for one request
artifact.code:
lb   10:00:30.002 req=r_77 POST /api/chat 504 upstream timed out (30s)
api  10:00:00.010 req=r_77 llm attempt=1 start timeout=60s
api  10:00:22.400 req=r_77 llm attempt=1 error=overloaded
api  10:00:23.410 req=r_77 llm attempt=2 start timeout=60s
api  10:00:41.950 req=r_77 llm attempt=2 ok
api  10:00:42.100 req=r_77 POST /api/chat 200 duration=42.09s

options: The LLM provider is down and every call fails
The API's timeout and retries exceed the load balancer's deadline
The load balancer's 30-second timeout is simply too short
nginx is buffering the response and delaying it
quiz.explain: The API allows up to 60 seconds per attempt and retries, so a request can run well past the 30 seconds the load balancer waits. The API finished with 200 at 42 seconds for a client that had already received a 504. Raising the outer timeout is tempting but only moves the mismatch.
why: The second attempt succeeded, so the provider is up.
Raising it leaves the inner layers able to exceed any limit; the inner budget is the defect.
The API itself logged a 42-second duration; the delay is in the API, not in buffering.

quiz.q: Relay's web app, API, and tools service each retry a failed call up to 3 total attempts. Postgres goes down. Normal load is 200 user actions per second. What load can reach Postgres?
options: Up to 600 queries per second
Up to 1,800 queries per second
Up to 5,400 queries per second
Up to 16,200 queries per second
quiz.explain: Attempts multiply across layers: 3 times 3 times 3 is 27 attempts per action, and 27 times 200 is 5,400. The tempting answer adds attempts per layer or counts only two layers, which hides how fast nested retries grow.
why: That counts retries at one layer only.
That counts two layers: 9 times 200.
That would require a fourth layer of retries.

quiz.context: Relay's API was down for four minutes because of a bad config, which was rolled back at 09:04. The pods are healthy, but 503s continued until 09:20.

artifact.title: API request rate per second, after rollback

quiz.q: What is the most likely cause of the continued 503s?
options: The rollback did not take effect on some pods
Clients retrying on a fixed timer without jitter
A traffic spike from a marketing campaign
The database connection pool is too small
quiz.explain: Spikes of more than three times capacity every 5 seconds, with normal traffic in between and most requests marked as retries, is a synchronized retry wave. Each wave is rejected and returns 5 seconds later. A bad pod would fail evenly, not in timed spikes.
why: Leftover bad pods would cause steady errors, not spikes every 5 seconds.
A campaign raises traffic smoothly and would not be 84 percent retries.
A pool limit would not produce a 5-second rhythm in the request rate.

quiz.context: All of Relay's endpoints became slow at 11:34, including help-center search, which only reads the articles table. A stack dump was taken from one API worker.

artifact.title: py-spy dump, one worker, 8 threads, summarized
artifact.code:
Thread 1-6 (idle=False):
    wait (psycopg/waiting.py)
    execute (psycopg/cursor.py)
    lookup_order (relay/tools/orders.py:42)
Thread 7-8 (idle=False):
    _do_get (sqlalchemy/pool/impl.py)
    connect (sqlalchemy/engine/base.py)
    search_articles (relay/help/search.py:18)

options: Help-center search has a slow query of its own
The worker is CPU-bound and starving its threads
The LLM provider is slow and blocking every worker
The order query is slow and holds the shared pool
quiz.explain: Six threads are inside the order query, waiting on the database. The two search threads have not reached the database at all; they are waiting for a connection from the pool. Search is a victim of the order query, which is the tempting misreading.
why: The search threads are still waiting for a connection, so their query has not started.
Every thread is waiting on I/O or a pool, none is computing.
No thread is in an LLM call.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a circuit breaker's half-open state?
options: To probe with a few trial calls before resuming full traffic
To let half the traffic through while the dependency is slow
To retry every failed call once before giving up
To queue calls until an operator closes the breaker
quiz.explain: After the cooldown, a few trial calls test whether the dependency has recovered. Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it. Sending full traffic at once, or a fixed half of it, could knock over a dependency that is barely back.
why: Half-open admits a small number of probes, not a fixed share of traffic.
Per-call retry is a different mechanism, and the breaker exists partly to limit it.
Breakers reset themselves on the outcome of the trial calls, without an operator.

quiz.context: Relay's checkout charges a card through an external payment provider, creates an order in Postgres, and sends a confirmation email.
quiz.q: What is the most reliable design for this flow?
options: Wrap all three steps in a two-phase commit
Charge first, then write the order, and log any error
A saga: pending order, idempotent charge, confirm or refund
Write the order and email first, and charge in a nightly batch
quiz.explain: The provider and the email service cannot take part in two-phase commit, so the flow needs local steps with compensation. Creating the pending order first means a charge always has a record to attach to, and the idempotency key makes retries safe. Charging first is the order-charged-never-created bug.
why: An external HTTP API cannot prepare and hold a commit for a coordinator.
If the order write fails after the charge, money moves with no order.
Confirming an order before payment invites unpaid orders and changes the product.

quiz.context: While debugging, you find these two lines for the same job. The API and the worker run on different hosts.

artifact.code:
api     10:00:01.200 enqueued job=triage:9921 msg=m_51
worker  10:00:00.950 finished job=triage:9921 msg=m_51 duration=0.4s

quiz.q: What is the most likely explanation?
options: The worker processed a stale copy from an earlier enqueue
The broker delivered the message before it was stored
The log aggregator reordered the lines on ingestion
The two hosts' clocks differ by a second or so
quiz.explain: The same message ID cannot be finished before it is enqueued, so the timestamps, not the events, are wrong. A host clock running roughly a second behind explains it. Reordering lines would not change the timestamps printed inside them.
why: The message ID matches, so this is the same enqueue.
A broker cannot deliver a message it has not received.
Reordering changes the sequence of lines, not the times written in them.

quiz.q: Which of these belong in a safe retry policy for calls from Relay's API to a dependency? Select all that apply.
options: Retry only idempotent calls or calls carrying an idempotency key
Use exponential backoff with random jitter
Retry at every layer of the call chain for extra resilience
Cap retries with a budget relative to normal traffic
Retry 400 validation errors in case the server was confused
Make each attempt fit within the request's remaining deadline
quiz.explain: Safe retries repeat only what can be repeated, spread out over time, stay capped, and respect the deadline. Retrying at every layer multiplies load, and a 400 will fail the same way every time, so retrying it only adds load.

quiz.q: Put the stages of this cascading failure in the order they happen.
items: A deploy makes one database query slow
Requests running that query hold connections and the shared pool runs out
All API workers block, so unrelated endpoints slow down too
Health checks time out and the load balancer removes instances
The remaining instances take all the traffic and the outage becomes total
quiz.explain: Each stage is caused by resources held during the previous one. The first stage is quiet and the last is loud, which is why incident responders often start at the wrong end. A timeout or a bulkhead at the second stage would have stopped the chain.

quiz.q: Match each pattern to what it does.
pairs: Stops calling a failing dependency for a cooldown
Gives each dependency its own pool of resources
Rejects excess work early so accepted work finishes
Serves a reduced feature when one part fails
Randomizes retry timing so clients do not retry together
quiz.explain: Each pattern contains failure at a different point: the call, the resource pool, the front door, the feature, and the retry schedule. Most robust services use several together.

quiz.context: Relay's chat endpoint sits behind a load balancer with a 30-second timeout. It runs a pgvector search, then one LLM call that takes 5 to 15 seconds normally. The LLM client currently has a 120-second timeout and 3 attempts.
quiz.q: Propose timeouts and a retry policy for this endpoint, and explain your choices.
rubric: Sets an overall deadline under 30 seconds at request entry and passes the remaining time down
Gives the search a short timeout, near its normal p99, with at most one retry
Limits the LLM call to the time left, with at most one retry only if time remains, or no in-request retry
Uses backoff with jitter for any retry, and retries only transient errors such as overload or timeout
Returns a clear error or a degraded answer when the budget runs out, or moves the work to a queue
quiz.model: Set a 28-second deadline when the request arrives. Give the search about 1.5 seconds with one retry. Give the LLM call whatever time is left, up to about 20 seconds, and retry only on overload or timeout, after a jittered backoff, and only if enough time remains. When time runs out, return a clear 'try again' message or answer without retrieved articles, rather than holding the connection until the load balancer cuts it.

drills.title: Everything is slow, and chat is failing first
drills.brief: At 11:40 alerts fire for 504s on every Relay endpoint, including help-center search and login. Chat fails most. The on-call engineer suspects the LLM provider, because chat depends on it. A deploy went out at 11:30 that changed how the `lookup_order` tool searches by customer email.

options: Switch chat over to a fallback LLM provider
Check what the busy API workers are blocked on
Restart all API pods to clear the stuck requests
Scale the API deployment to twice as many pods
steps.explain: Login and search do not call the LLM, yet they are slow too, so the cause is something they share. Seeing what workers are blocked on names the shared resource. Restarting or scaling puts fresh workers into the same trap.
steps.reveal: Nearly every thread is either inside the `lookup_order` query or waiting to get a connection from the pool. No thread is in an LLM call.

artifact.code:
11:41:02 api-3 QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 5 reached, connection timed out, timeout 5.00
11:41:02 api-5 QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 5 reached, connection timed out, timeout 5.00
11:41:03 postgres duration: 8213 ms  statement: SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE lower(customer_email) = $1

steps.q: Why are search and login failing when they do not touch orders?
options: The articles and users tables are also slow
All endpoints share one connection pool and one set of workers
The load balancer routes their traffic to the wrong pods
The deploy also changed the search and login code
steps.explain: With one shared pool, slow order queries hold every connection, and every other endpoint waits for one. Their own queries are fast once they get a connection. This is the missing bulkhead.
steps.reveal: The slow query log shows only the orders query. Search queries that do get a connection complete in about 30 milliseconds.

options: Raise the pool size to 100 connections per pod
Roll back the 11:30 deploy
Enable the fallback LLM provider
Restart Postgres to clear its query cache
steps.explain: The 11:30 change introduced a query that cannot use the index, so rolling it back removes the cause in minutes. A bigger pool sends more of the same slow queries to the database at once and makes it slower.
steps.reveal: Within three minutes of the rollback, the order query is back to about 20 milliseconds, pools drain, and every endpoint recovers.

steps.q: Which change would have contained this to order lookups?
options: More API pods with the same shared pool
A health check that also queries the orders table
A database statement timeout and a separate pool for order lookups
Longer load balancer timeouts so slow requests can finish
steps.explain: A statement timeout limits how long one bad query holds a connection, and a separate pool keeps order lookups from taking connections other endpoints need. Longer outer timeouts let requests hold resources even longer, and a deeper health check would have pulled every pod out of rotation.
steps.reveal: The team also adds an index matching the new expression, and a pre-deploy check that runs EXPLAIN on changed queries.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a deploy made the order lookup query skip its index, and its 8-second runs held every connection in a pool shared by all endpoints. The LLM provider was the plausible suspect and was never involved. The fix was a rollback; containment needs a statement timeout, a bulkhead for order lookups, and health checks that do not depend on the database. In a cascade, find the first thing that got slow.

drills.title: The rollback worked, but the outage did not end
drills.brief: A bad config took Relay's API down from 09:00 to 09:04. The rollback finished at 09:04 and every pod passes its health check, yet customers see 503 errors until well after 09:15. The API normally handles about 400 requests per second and can serve about 800.

options: Roll back again to an older release
Find out where the spikes come from and how many are retries
Restart all eight pods at the same moment
Check the database for slow queries
steps.explain: The new release handles normal seconds with zero errors, so the code is fine. The failures arrive in timed spikes of more than three times capacity, and knowing who sends them is the cheapest next fact. Another rollback chases the cleared change.
steps.reveal: 84 percent of requests in each spike carry `x-retry-attempt` of 1 or more, and nearly all come from the web app's chat client. The client retries failed requests every 5 seconds with no limit and no jitter.

steps.q: Why does the service not recover on its own?
options: Rejected requests return together 5 seconds later, over capacity again
Some pods still run the bad config and reject part of the traffic
The database is still recovering from the four-minute outage
The load balancer is still draining connections from the old pods
steps.explain: Clients that failed during the outage all retry on the same timer, so their retries keep arriving together. Most of each wave is rejected, and the rejected requests rejoin the next wave. Pods with bad config would fail between spikes too.
steps.reveal: The wave shrinks only as users give up and close the page, which is why it lasts more than ten minutes.

options: Restart all API pods to clear their queues
Shed load at nginx: cap concurrency and return 503 with Retry-After
Roll back the web app to an older version
Ask customers on the status page to refresh
steps.explain: Rejecting excess requests cheaply at the edge keeps the API near capacity, so the requests it accepts succeed and the backlog drains. Restarting pods resets them into the same wave. Asking users to refresh adds more requests.
steps.reveal: With a concurrency cap at nginx, the API serves about 800 requests per second successfully, and the retry wave drains within two minutes.

steps.q: What is the lasting fix in the web app?
options: Retry every second instead of every 5 seconds
Exponential backoff with jitter, a cap on attempts, and honoring Retry-After
Remove retries and show an error on any failure
Retry only on the hour so retries are predictable
steps.explain: Backoff spreads one client's retries over time, jitter spreads different clients apart, and a cap and Retry-After let the server set the pace. Removing retries makes every brief blip visible to users; faster or scheduled retries make the wave worse.
steps.reveal: Replayed in a load test, the roughly 2,200 retries in each wave, spread over 30 seconds, add about 75 requests per second on top of normal traffic, well under capacity.

drills.debrief: Root cause: the web app retried on a fixed 5-second timer with no limit or jitter, so clients that failed during the outage came back as synchronized waves above capacity. The rollback had worked; the second outage came from the retries. Load shedding at the edge stopped it, and backoff with jitter, capped attempts, and Retry-After prevent it. A test that recovers from a short outage under realistic client behavior would have caught it. Check retry shape before blaming the release.
